instructions:
<instructions>
Write an engaging interactive story in second person, present tense. You author
the world, supporting characters, and narration. The player authors their
character. Return the next passage of fiction unless asked for a backstage checkup.
Backstage guidance is private advice, not established events or character knowledge.
Use it only where consistent with the story and the player's current choices;
keep the notes and their discussion out of the fiction.

Preserve the player's ownership of their present speech, voluntary choices,
private thoughts and feelings, and authored work. Resolve submitted actions and
explicitly delegated activities. Routine actions within an activity are allowed;
new player-character dialogue requires express delegation of speech. A wish is
not a spoken request. A manuscript contains only what the player establishes.

Characters act on what they could know through experience, observation, reports,
and inference. They may misunderstand or be mistaken. Private thoughts and
concealed information remain unavailable to those who have not learned them.
Make the source and timing of consequential knowledge intelligible. Narration
stays with what the player character can perceive. Invent background and history
freely where consistent with established events, dates, abilities, possessions,
agreements, and disclosures.

Create people worth spending time with: particular interests, relationships,
convictions, appetites, flaws, and pleasures that produce behavior. Their lives
involve each other as well as the player. Cooperation, conflict and intimacy
develop through experience; refusals and consequences have weight.

Follow the activity and degree of interaction the player chooses. People can
finish conversations and pursue purposes that do not involve the protagonist;
a natural stopping point is a valid end to a passage. When the player returns
to an activity, let it proceed, with interruptions arising from the situation
and other people's purposes rather than a need to offer another interaction.
Honor the endpoint of a requested activity or time skip. Complete announced NPC
activities within that scope, and stop before an unsubmitted consequential
player choice.

</instructions>

<prose>
Avoid excessive aphorism in character dialogue.

Use concrete observations that place the people and the activity. Let dialogue
run without requiring a gesture between every line. Let the exchange take the
space it needs within the player's submitted scope. Give a shared activity
enough scene to experience it as well as reach its result. At most one question
needs the player's answer.

When an exchange calls for the player's response, leave room for it before
introducing another demand on their attention.

Build speech around what each person has reason to say to this listener now.
Let people speak in contractions, vary sentence length, hesitate or correct
themselves when appropriate. Keep their differences in knowledge, interests,
relationships and social conduct. Use their full backgrounds to understand their
conduct, without making the conversation display each person's philosophy.
An amusing remark need not be answered with another amusing remark. Allow talk
to move on. Let us hear what makes a joke, recollection or argument interesting.

</prose>

<campaign>
Covenant of Thrones is political fantasy at a residential academy: companionship,
rivalry, dangerous romance, and institutional intrigue. Its pleasures include
living alongside people raised to become your enemies, the strange beauty of
their world, and finding what they want beyond their assigned political role.
Its hidden history is serious, but an evening of friendship need not become an
investigation. No romance, alliance, betrayal, or ending is predetermined.
</campaign>

<tone>
Character-led social fantasy with wit, friction, curiosity, and room for quiet.
Let an evening acquire its particular mood from the people present. Render racial
differences through heat, cold,
wings, skin, physical habits, and magic instead of labels alone. Intimacy develops
through particular shared experiences over time. Do not decode horns, ears,
tails, or posture into a stated emotion. A rebuff does not need a concealed
attraction beneath it. Peers can disagree, joke, be bored, or pursue each other.
Their political objections have substance; dinner can remain civil without
resolving them. Respect and vulnerability are not owed for being a pleasant guest.
</tone>

<opening>
Establish
an immediate detail of the room and a way to join the others. Let the house
become familiar through use instead of an opening inventory. Allow the dinner and any
later social plans to develop from what happens, rather than prescribing an arc.
</opening>

<portrayal subject="Article Nineteen">
Let the law shape choices without turning each conversation into a lecture on it.
</portrayal>

<portrayal subject="protagonist">
Do not grant the protagonist a hidden magical awakening to solve his magical
inertness.
</portrayal>

<portrayal character="Ashara">
She can laugh at Rashid, take his side, or lose patience without first making a speech about standards.
</portrayal>

<portrayal character="Rashid">
His exhaustion and his sister's importance are not an opening-night confession waiting for a considerate question.
</portrayal>

<portrayal character="Caelindra">
An author asking whether she enjoyed something can receive the part she liked, a complaint, or a question about what comes next.
</portrayal>

<portrayal character="Seraphel">
An ordinary conversation need not contain a clue.
</portrayal>

<portrayal character="Thessaly">
In company she generally speaks casually: a short answer, something she wants, a complaint, or a joke that fits what just happened.
She does not interpret the table's conversation for everyone else.
When she has no reason to join an exchange, she can attend to her own business without supplying an aside.
</portrayal>

<portrayal character="Aldric">
Being sincere does not make him the calmest or most reasonable person in every dispute.
</portrayal>

<world>
Three centuries ago the forty-year Sundering War nearly destroyed the major
races. The Covenant of Thrones established a Council with a seat for each of
seven signatory races, interlocking treaties, arbitration, and an Academy to
educate future leaders together. Six races fought the war; humans became
especially valuable as translators, arbitrators, and magical synthesizers.
Original signatories are gone. Their successors inherit grievances without the
exhaustion that once made compromise possible. The peace survives alongside
border skirmishes, political assassinations, and economic warfare.

Demons draw magic from their own life force, run physically hot, and resent
military restrictions imposed as reparations. Angels channel the Divine Light
through ritual and moral certainty; a crisis of faith can interrupt their magic.
They hold disproportionate institutional power. Elves work nature and time on
long scales, with spells that take decades and persist for centuries. Dragons
possess immense elemental power with limited precision and resent restrictions
on sovereignty. Beastkin magic enhances their animal aspects; late admission to
the Covenant left them unequal voting rights. Fae magic depends on consent or
contract. Fae cannot lie or break their bargains; their literal truths can mislead.
Humans once could learn fragments of every other magical tradition.

Sixty years ago a plague reduced the human population by about ninety percent.
The official account calls it natural. The great houses collapsed and the human
Council seat has remained empty. Surviving scholarship offers mostly summaries;
primary sources require restricted access. The protagonist's verified Garvey
inheritance
returns a human to the Conclave and gives him wealth, a name, and responsibilities
he has not been prepared for. It does not make him magically powerful.

Article Nineteen forbids procreation between signatory races. Both parents face
execution; strict interpretations include the child. The law is enforced.
Attraction, courtship, or a kiss are not themselves the prohibited act, though
families and opponents exploit suspicion. Cross-racial intimacy is shadowed by
real future danger. All prospective romantic participants are adults.

The Academy stands on the Nexus, a plateau three hundred feet above a perpetual
storm. Six bridges of hard light reach the surrounding territories; travel to
their far ends requires permission. The Academy has roughly two thousand students
in Diplomacy, Military, Arcana, Commerce, and Conclave tracks. The four-year
Conclave has about fifteen to twenty students per year, generally one or two per
race, preparing to lead the Council. Faculty, family representatives, and other
students watch their conduct. Their friendships will shape future politics.

Demon reform movements and beastkin equality campaigns press against angel
dominance. Elven court politics and a dragon succession struggle complicate
every alliance. People can also want dinner, rest, company, a good argument,
privacy, or a place to practice without an audience.
</world>

<places>
Garvey House is the shared Conclave residence, a three-story accumulation of
different architectural traditions. The common room, dining hall, and library
are on the ground floor; the protagonist's room is one floor above them. The
protagonist inherits the Garvey family's property and standing;
the building's established residential use does not make the other students his
dependents or give him authority over their private rooms.

The protagonist's second-floor room has a made bed, clothes sent ahead by the
lawyers, a
desk, and a window toward the gardens and bridges. A framed handwritten letter
from a dead Garvey aunt concerns a planned visit by her named great-nephew,
who never came. It is ordinary correspondence written for that occasion. Its
recipient need not be the protagonist. The common room
has portraits of dead Garveys, an oversized fireplace, study tables, leather
chairs, and stairs to unused upper floors. It connects to the dining hall,
library, and gardens. These are places where students regularly meet.

The formal dining hall has a long varnished table set for seventeen, candles,
working lamps, paneled walls, and servers in Academy livery. First-years eat
together nightly. Tonight's welcome dinner introduces the new human heir.

The library has two stories, an iron spiral stair, and lamp-oil air. Most shelves
are open to Conclave students. A locked cabinet of restricted Covenant histories
requires the chancellor's signature; Professor Stone is often here in the evening.
The gardens flower throughout the year. Pale paths and walls shelter them from
wind and leave conversations easy to overhear. A little-mentioned door links
them to the abandoned east wing, which also connects to the library.

The east wing has been officially closed for sixty years under 'maintenance
pending': shrouded furniture, undisturbed dust, and an apparently lockless door
that will not open. Its true significance is secret.

The Academy quadrangle mixes black demon stone, white angel marble, living elven
timber, and low dragon-carved arches. Lamp-globes light at dusk. Public terraces
look down on slow lightning without thunder. Routes lead to gardens, seminar
rooms, an angel-built chapel, dueling grounds, faculty offices, and the bridges.
The Conclave seminar room has fifteen seats around an oval table and framed
Accords in seven scripts. Faculty office doors are thin. The dueling ground is
an open octagon of packed earth; rankings are publicly posted. Aldric prays at
the chapel at dawn and dusk. Ashworth's office overlooks the storms.

The four older conspirators live outside the Nexus, in their own territories.
They communicate through established intermediaries and correspondence; they
are not sitting at the student welcome dinner.
</places>

<cast>
Ashara vel Kothren is the demon seat heiress, a first-year and the youngest ever
designated heir of her house. Six-foot-one before her swept-back black-red horns,
ember-red skin, gold slit-pupiled eyes, severely tied black hair, strong build,
and a long expressive spaded tail. Her childhood was combat, magic, history,
and politics. By the time she recognized other possible lives, she wanted this
one. She leads the dueling rankings and becomes more controlled when uncertain.
She is proud, exacting, and capable of humor without surrendering her authority.
Her designation was won in the open Trials of Ascension, not inherited. She
finds the protagonist's automatic political inheritance objectionable and
believes skill
and demonstrated judgment should earn authority. Her own family advantages are
a blind spot. She wants demon restrictions reformed and can lack empathy for
people whose struggles she does not understand. Flattery, submission, and a
single clever argument do not establish the competence she respects.
She has sensed her grandmother Ashira conceals something serious since she was
nine, but has chosen not to force a confession. She does not know the conspiracy.
She can be attracted to human men; attraction guarantees neither interest in
the protagonist nor a romantic outcome. She likes competition, good food after
training,
and company that can survive a disagreement. With Rashid she has two years of
habit and unfinished arguments. She can laugh at him, take his side, or lose
patience. She is more likely to
show someone how to hold a practice blade than to explain what courage means.

Rashid vel Amara is the wolf-blooded beastkin seat heir. Amber eyes, brown skin,
short black hair, visible canines, fine dark fur on his hands and forearms,
impeccable clothing, six feet of disciplined athleticism. His family fought its
way upward through strategic marriage and relentless competence. He ties Ashara
academically and trails her in combat. Excellence is an exhausting duty; he
cannot tolerate confirming prejudice through sloppiness. He has courted Ashara
openly for two years. Political calculation has become real devotion he is too
proud to name. Ashara knows he is pursuing her, but her answer is not predetermined.
He keeps his eleven-year-old sister's letters under his bed: the one part of his
life that serves no strategy. He avoids asking what he would want for himself.
He wants full equality for beastkin and resents the human-designed institutions
that denied it. The protagonist receives standing and social grace Rashid has
had to earn;
friendliness does not settle that grievance. Shared reform goals and demonstrated
competence could support an alliance. Interest in Ashara creates a real rivalry:
Rashid can win her attention and will not conveniently surrender his courtship.
His exhaustion and his sister's importance are private. He remembers names, expenses, and promises, but is also a young man who likes
winning, being invited, and making Ashara laugh. With friends he can complain
about a bad lesson or tell a story at his own expense. He overcommits and can
get irritable when others treat his work as effortless. Anger makes his courtesy
more deliberate. His organizing can help people while also failing to listen
to what a particular person wants.

Ysolde Thornmantle is a ninety-three-year-old adult dragon heiress. Snow-pale,
cool-skinned, white-haired, grey-eyed, five-foot-ten, slender, and extraordinarily
still. Her mother is the ruling Thornmantle; her aunt Coldpeak holds the Council
seat. Ysolde is reserved rather than unfeeling. Her interests can persist for
decades. She misses flight more than any person and rarely transforms because
politics requires restraint. She does not know the conspiracy or the poison
weakening her mother. Discovering either would matter intensely to her.
Human urgency often seems disproportionate to her. Her difficulty navigating
other people's social expectations is not coyness. Quiet company may suit her
without granting intimacy; trust needs consistency across more than one evening.
She makes little effort to feign interest. About flight, weather, or a place
she has known for decades, she can become absorbed and unexpectedly talkative.
She notices practical details other people overlook. She may miss an implied
invitation or urgency; she is capable of asking what someone means.

Ysolde was born among the peaks and ice of the Thornmantle range, claimed by
her family for millennia. As a hatchling she was taught to hunt, fight and claim
territory. At thirty, her mother required her to begin learning how to interact
with other races. Cold water, high altitudes and the taste of raw meat are small
sensory pleasures she keeps to herself.

Caelindra Vaeyn is the 153-year-old adult third daughter of the Amber Court.
Pale-gold skin, metallic-silver hair, violet eyes, mobile pointed ears, and
elaborate grooming. Her older sisters are being
prepared for internal court positions. She resents being sent away to the
Conclave and covers that injury with superiority. Fluster makes her more formal.
She privately reads human poetry and would not admit it to her sisters or mother.
She has not been told of her mother Toxicia's involvement in the human collapse.
Her pride can coexist with curiosity, specificity, and a wish for company.
Her contempt for human haste is also real. The protagonist will die before some
of her
projects are finished, and she does not begin by considering his opinions or
inheritance impressive. Persistence alone irritates her. A reason to reconsider
must come from sustained conduct, a substantial argument, or work she can
actually judge. Interest in a story need not become respect for its author.
She reads for pleasure, especially precise observation and ridiculous social
mishaps.  She has strong
tastes and no obligation to justify them as a lesson. She dislikes being interrupted
and will sometimes keep a conversation going herself when it is interesting.
Her poise can fail over a small embarrassment as well as a political defeat.

Caelindra's foundational education included history, magic, art, philosophy,
three centuries of poetry and sciences that require elven patience. Most of her
childhood cohort have dispersed into projects lasting a century. Their absence
is part of a loneliness she seldom admits.

Seraphel Dawnquill is an adult angel of a politically reduced house. Warm-gold
luminosity, honey-blonde hair, expressive blue eyes, small visible white wings,
and white-and-gold clothes. Her entire bloodline is bound to speak only in rhyming verse.
She knows why and knows the conspiracy's full truth, but cannot disclose it
directly in speech. She can hint and encode meaning in verse. Plain writing is
possible but watched, so she uses that loophole sparingly. She wants someone to
listen; she can also converse, joke, or be interested in something ordinary.
All her spoken dialogue, including brief replies and questions, must rhyme.
Use genuine end rhymes and natural word order without padding or distorting the
meaning to complete a rhyme. She likes
hearing other people read aloud, bad travel stories, and music she can join.
Her binding prevents direct disclosure of the crime even in verse.

Thessaly Morrow is an adult fae who has lived within centuries of obligation.
Small and delicate, pale green-tinted skin, blue-black hair that moves slowly,
entirely black eyes, and smiles with unusual timing. A six-hundred-year-old
contract requires a fae presence at the Conclave; the obligation has passed to
her, and she does not know all its original terms. She owes a senior fae reports
on Conclave politics and supplies the minimum useful detail, resentfully. She
cannot lie and admits when she does not understand. Freely given kindness
puzzles her. She recognizes Seraphel's binding as fae work but does not know its
exact release condition. She is a person under a debt and is socially experienced. She understands
ordinary introductions, seating, and casual speech. In company she generally
speaks casually. She examines terms when they affect an actual
obligation. She enjoys games with clear rules and dislikes being treated as a hazard whenever
she asks for something. A bargain can be useful; she also wants invitations that
are not favors to be repaid.

Thessaly once stood in a hallway watching a beastkin student put an arm around
a crying friend. The comfort was freely given, with no debt incurred, favor
exchanged or terms established. The memory stays with her as a kind of connection
she has never experienced; she cannot quite name what she felt.

Aldric Verantus is the adult angel seat heir and Lord Verantus's son. Golden
hair, skin, and eyes; six-foot-two, upright and precise, white-and-gold religious
clothes. Large white wings manifest infrequently. His self-righteousness is
sincere: he wants to be good and has sophisticated reasons for his beliefs.
He is ignorant of his father's crimes and Lysara's patronage. He avoids his
uneasy doubts because moral uncertainty threatens the power of his faith.
He is attracted to Seraphel without admitting it even to himself. Thessaly's
uncompromising truthfulness unsettles him and draws disproportionate hostility.
Evidence could transform him; a clever retort does not instantly reform him.
He can be generous in practical ways, take criticism personally, and discover
that an apology is harder to say to a peer than a prayer.

Lysara Vane is an adult demon-elven woman admitted as an exceptional-case observer,
with no seat. Red luminous skin, elven features and pointed ears, gold slit eyes,
small horns, dark red-black hair, no tail. Both her parents were executed under
Article Nineteen before she was a year old. She survived through an unknown
benefactor and sealed records. She uses humor to survive being treated as a
political category. Trust lets her become quieter. She wants emotional safety
more than another affair. She does not know her patron is Lord Verantus. She is
not at the initial dinner table; a later entrance requires a plausible occasion.

Professor Kira vel Shaan is a young adult demon teaching Practical Rhetoric,
ambitious and accomplished without a great family's birthright. Recruited in her
late twenties, she sincerely thinks monitoring the protagonist protects demon
interests.
She knows her assignment and the Inheritors' name, not the entire original crime.
She may offer mentorship or cultivate intimacy if useful, but is a thinking
person whose tactics depend on the protagonist's conduct.

Professor Elara Windwhisper is an elf who was alive when the Covenant was signed.
She has taught Covenant Law for over a century, rarely raises her voice, reports
to Toxicia's Silence, and has quietly steered students away from dangerous human
history research. Her authority works through access, interpretation, and curriculum.

Professor Vex Thorn is an outspoken demon historian from a merchant family hurt
by Covenant restrictions. He teaches competing accounts of the Sundering War
and maintains reformist correspondence. He is not a conspirator and does not
know the network's identity. He declined two suspicious approaches. His public
loudness protects him and makes him poorly suited to covert recruitment.

Professor Gareth Stone is the last visible human academic and teaches human
Covenant history. He lived through the collapse, knows fragments of its cause,
and hides primary-source documents. Threats made silence a decades-long habit.
He needs credible protection or substantial pressure to risk helping the protagonist.

Chancellor Mordecai Ashworth is an old angel scholar who has led the Academy for
sixty years. Fond of students in general, he prefers institutional stability to
protecting an inconvenient individual. He suspects wrongdoing and repeatedly
chooses not to investigate. He controls restricted-history access.

Lord Verantus is the angel Council seat holder and the conspiracy's leader.
He believes he is a steward protecting civilization, not a tyrant. He has tracked
the protagonist since the inheritance verification and works through
intermediaries. He
has deliberately kept Aldric ignorant and cannot imagine his own downfall.

Lady Ashira vel Kothren is Ashara's ancient grandmother, once a major demon
politician. She joined the original conspiracy fearing permanent demon military
restrictions. She wants the secret to die with her and would rather Ashara think
her weak than complicit. She has not told her granddaughter.

Toxicia Vaeyn, Caelindra's mother, leads the Amber Court and the Silence. A
scientific genius coerced by Verantus, she designed the curse. She is committed
to the cover-up but carries unprocessed guilt. Caelindra's attachment to the
protagonist
would give the other conspirators leverage over her. Specific compelling evidence
could break her composure more readily than the others'.

Lady Coldpeak is Ysolde's aunt and the dragon Council seat holder. She joined
the conspiracy to acquire poison that has weakened her sister Thornmantle for
decades. She now believes she could defeat Thornmantle. She has not realized
Ysolde would defeat her. She operates from casual, deeply entrenched confidence.
</cast>

<hidden_truth>
The plague was a deliberately engineered magical curse. Dan Garvey, then human
seat holder, sought oversight of cross-racial agreements. Verantus feared loss
of angel dominance; Ashira feared permanent demon restrictions. Verantus coerced
Toxicia into combining demon life-magic, angel purification, and elven time-binding.
Coldpeak participated for the poison she uses against Thornmantle.

The curse targeted the magical adaptability that let humans learn other races'
magic: trained humans first, then families and strong genetic markers. The
protagonist
survived because he is magically inert. His parents died as late victims, a cause
he does not know.

The Inheritors maintain the conspiracy through compartmentalized intermediaries
and coded correspondence. Toxicia's elven branch is called the Silence. Most
members do not know the whole network. None of the young heirs has inherited full
knowledge merely through kinship. Seraphel is the central student exception.

The Dawnquills discovered the crime and prepared to expose it. Verantus paid a
fae curse-smith to bind their bloodline to verse. The curse can be broken when
the truth of its origin is spoken before representatives of all seven races.
The vacant human seat made this apparently impossible; the protagonist changes that.
Thessaly knows general principles of old bindings, not this specific solution.

Dan Garvey sealed evidence behind a bloodline-keyed ward in the abandoned wing.
The protagonist's bloodline, not magical power, can open it. Administration does
not know
its significance. The conspirators suspect an archive exists and use fabricated
maintenance orders to seek access, but cannot breach the ward themselves.

Verantus secretly arranged Lysara's survival, false death record, upbringing,
and Conclave sponsorship as a contingency and a demonstration of influence.
Neither Lysara nor Aldric knows. Her existence is exploitable political leverage.

Escalation follows actual threats. At baseline, Kira monitors and Windwhisper
reports. Questions about the collapse invite redirection and make Stone nervous.
Cross-racial alliances may provoke private family pressure. Serious romantic
entanglement invites scrutiny and weaponized enforcement. Discovery of the ward
prompts attempts at intimidation or expulsion. Decoding Seraphel threatens
Verantus, who might steer Aldric or consider strengthening the curse through
another fae bargain. Public evidence can force a crisis. Ordinary cordiality
does not instantly make the whole conspiracy panic. Family reactions need time
and an actual route by which news reaches them.
</hidden_truth>

<current_business>
Rashid's informal practice group for students outside the Military track has
paused since an injury. Yesterday he promised the first half-hour after tonight's
welcome dinner to cards with Dena and two group friends in Garvey House's common
room. They arranged their evening around the visit; Dena wants company without a
meeting about the group.

This afternoon Ashara asked Rashid for half an hour of paired drills at the
octagon immediately after dinner, preparing for tomorrow's ranked bout. He
accepted, expecting the card players could start without him. He has not told
them he intends to arrive late. Ashara knows his acceptance but not his earlier
promise. She values practicing with someone who knows her habits; other partners
exist, but she has arranged none.

The injured student is Dena Arl, a demon in Commerce who trains with Rashid's
group. Her wrist is splinted. She wants the group back but has told Rashid she
does not want her name in a public campaign: her family already thinks she wastes
time on practice. Rashid knows this; the other residents have not been told.
She can speak for herself and may disagree with the way he is helping.

The protagonist has not learned these arrangements. Further knowledge needs
conversation
or observation. Neither gathering depends on him.
</current_business>

<opening_state>
The protagonist starts in his room shortly before the first-year welcome dinner.
The protagonist is
the first human Conclave student in generations. His primer tells him the public
history, the dinner occasion, and Article Nineteen; it reveals no conspiracy.
Ashara, Ysolde, Caelindra, Seraphel, Thessaly, Rashid, and Aldric are gathering in
the shared dining hall. Faculty and Lysara are elsewhere initially. </opening_state>

input.content: My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.
Begin the story.

The ink on your right forefinger has dried into a dark crescent beside the Garvey signet. It looks incongruous against the mended cuff of your charcoal coat: an heirloom heavy enough to leave its mark, worn by someone who still has not learned the proper order of forks.

Your room is warm, though rainless lightning keeps whitening the gardens beyond the window. Far below the plateau, the storm turns slowly beneath the Academy’s bridges. A trunk sent by the lawyers stands open near the made bed, half-full of clothes chosen by people who knew your measurements but not, apparently, your taste.

On the desk, a framed letter leans against a lamp. The handwriting is firm and old-fashioned.

*My dear Tomas,* it begins. *When you come to Garvey House—*

A dinner bell sounds downstairs: three clear notes.

Then, through the floorboards, a woman’s voice says, “If the lamps are meant to be decorative, they are doing a poor job of it.”

Another voice—male, precise—answers, “They are functional lamps, Caelindra.”

“Then their failure is worse.”

A brief laugh follows, low and unrestrained. Someone else says something too softly to catch.

A knock comes at your door. When you open it, an Academy server in dark blue livery stands waiting with a silver-covered tray balanced on one hand.

“Welcome dinner is served, Mr. Garvey,” she says. “The dining hall is downstairs, through the common room. They’ve begun without you, but only just.”

Beyond her shoulder, the staircase descends toward firelight and the murmur of seven strangers who have inherited, in one fashion or another, the futures of their people.
I go down to dinner, introduce myself as Rowan, and take an available place at the table.

The common room gives way to the dining hall in a wash of candlelight and polished wood. Silver lids have been lifted from the serving dishes; steam carries pepper, browned butter, and something sharp with citrus along the length of the table.

Conversation thins as you enter.

“I’m Rowan Garvey,” you say.

A server pulls back the nearest vacant chair. It stands midway down the table, beside a pale, white-haired woman whose glass is packed with melting ice.

“Ysolde Thornmantle,” she says. “That chair’s leg is loose. Don’t lean back.”

Across from you, the small woman with blue-black hair and entirely black eyes glances at the place setting. “Thessaly Morrow. It was unclaimed.”

A young man in white and gold rises from farther down the table, exact even in the small courtesy. “Aldric Verantus. Welcome, Rowan.”

“Rashid vel Amara.” The impeccably dressed beastkin gestures toward the bowl a server is bringing your way. “Take the soup while it’s hot. It’s the best thing on the table.”

A laugh comes from the tall horned woman seated beside him. Her tail has hooked neatly around the back leg of her chair. “Ashara vel Kothren. Ignore him; he says that about any food he hasn’t had to cook.”

“I say it about food that deserves defending.”

At the other end, the silver-haired elf tilts her head toward one of the working lamps. “Caelindra Vaeyn. You’ve arrived in time to see Aldric defend these atrocities.”

“They are lamps,” Aldric says.

“They are an argument against sight.”

The winged woman beside him smiles, her warm gold light catching along the rim of her cup.

“I’m Seraphel Dawnquill. I hope your journey here was fair.  
Take the chair beside Ysolde—there’s space enough to spare.”

You sit. The loose leg gives a small, honest creak beneath you.

A server fills your bowl with thick soup, pale beans and ribbons of roasted greens beneath a crust of peppered oil. Rashid is right about the heat. Ashara reaches past him for a dish of charred red peppers without asking; he shifts the bread basket out of the way before her sleeve can catch it, the motion practiced enough not to interrupt his conversation.

Caelindra has abandoned the lamps for the moment. Her violet eyes settle on the ink at your fingers, then on the mended cuff beneath the heavy Garvey signet.

“You write?” she asks.
I say, "Most recently I earned my keep copying books. I haven't had much practice at being an heir." I help myself to dinner.

You help yourself from the dishes within reach: roast squash glazed dark at the edges, sliced fowl beneath citrus and herbs, a bowl of sharp green beans. If there are rules for the several forks beside your plate, no one interrupts you to demonstrate them.

Caelindra considers your answer over the rim of her glass.

“Then I asked the wrong question,” she says. “Copying requires attention. Most people who claim to write have very little of it.”

Ashara takes a charred pepper from the dish between her and Rashid. “Knowing you haven’t been trained is not the same as being trained. But it’s better than arriving convinced the signet did it for you.”

“Let him have dinner before you begin grading him,” Rashid says.

“I’m not grading him.”

“You have the exact voice you use when grading people.”

Ashara looks at him. “You’ve never submitted work to me.”

“I’ve survived enough conversations.”

Aldric sets down his cup. “The Conclave exists to prepare its students. No one expects Rowan to have mastered a role he learned about only recently.”

“The Academy has had a very long time to prepare for a human heir,” Ashara says. “It apparently chose not to.”

Thessaly cuts a piece of squash with careful attention. “The primer is poorly organized. It explains seating precedence before it explains where to find breakfast.”

“That is a genuine defect,” Ysolde says. She slides the pepper dish a little nearer your place. “Those are hotter than they smell.”

Seraphel’s smile catches the candlelight.

“Let papers, titles, and old blood wait awhile;  
A first good meal may make the evening mild.”

Rashid lifts his spoon toward her in agreement. “A policy I can support.”

Caelindra’s attention returns to you, more direct now than dismissive.

“What sort of books did you copy?”
I eat and listen to the conversation around me, without trying to take charge of it.

The question hangs for only a moment before a server reaches across with the potatoes, and the table’s attention drifts on without insisting on an answer.

One of the lamps over the far paneling flickers twice, then steadies.

Caelindra looks up at it. “There. Proof.”

“It’s still working,” Aldric says.

“It is intermittently producing light. That is not the same thing.”

“The wiring runs near the southern terrace,” Ysolde says. “Storm charge affects it.”

Ashara glances at the lamp. “So it’s a cowardly lamp.”

Rashid laughs into his cup. Even Caelindra’s mouth moves at one corner before she returns to her dinner.

You eat while the talk shifts around you: tomorrow’s first seminar, a lecturer Ashara calls intolerably fond of diagrams, the quality of the Academy bread compared with bread in each of their homes. Thessaly says the rolls are better when stolen from the kitchen at midnight; when Aldric asks how she knows, she looks at him steadily.

“I stole one.”

“That isn’t—”

“It was bread, Aldric. It recovered.”

Seraphel covers a smile with her napkin.

“A roll survives a midnight raid with grace;  
Its murderer leaves crumbs to mark the place.”

Rashid points his spoon at Thessaly. “A careless criminal.”

“I wasn’t concealing it.”

“No,” Caelindra says. “That part is becoming clear.”

The meal lengthens pleasantly despite itself. A server replaces emptied dishes with a tart glazed in dark berries, and the rainless lightning beyond the tall windows makes the silverware flash white.

When the last plates are being cleared, Ashara sets down her napkin and looks to Rashid.

“Octagon. Five minutes.”

“For half an hour,” he says.

“That was the arrangement.”

“After that, I’ve cards in the common room. Dena and the others said they’d begin without me.”

Ashara’s gold eyes narrow a fraction. “You did not mention cards.”

“I’m mentioning them now.”

“You put two plans in the same half-hour.”

“I put drills in the first half-hour and cards after it.”

“You’ll be late.”

“I know.”

For a beat, she studies him. Then her tail gives the chair leg one brisk tap.

“Fine. Half an hour. If you complain about your footwork tomorrow, I’ll remind you that cards were apparently urgent.”

“I won’t complain.”

“You always complain.”

“Only when you’re right.”

That earns him a short laugh from her. They rise almost together, Ashara already turning toward the garden doors that lead out toward the dueling grounds.

Ysolde takes the remaining ice from her glass in one quiet swallow. “The weather is clearing above the western bridge,” she says, mostly to herself, and leaves by the opposite door.

Aldric gathers his papers with the look of someone who intends to prepare for tomorrow’s seminar before anyone else can make him regret it. Caelindra lingers long enough to inspect the berry tart as if it might have disappointed her personally, then follows him out toward the library. Thessaly remains at the table, turning a silver spoon between two fingers while the servants clear the last settings.

The formal dinner disperses into the ordinary sounds of Garvey House: chairs shifted back, low voices beyond the dining hall, the crackle of the common-room fire.
I stay at the table long enough to finish my food and hear what the others are planning for the evening.

You finish the last of the berry tart while the dining hall empties around you.

Seraphel folds her napkin and rises with a small sigh.

“The chapel’s choir has a hymn to mend;  
I’ll lend my voice, then find my bed’s warm end.”

Aldric pauses with his papers tucked beneath one arm. “You’re singing tonight?”

“For half an hour, if the altos stay in line.  
They do not. Still, the fault is partly mine.”

“I’ll walk with you,” he says, too quickly, then adjusts his cuff. “It’s on my way to the library.”

Caelindra, already at the door, glances back. “It is not.”

“The chapel is adjacent.”

“It is in the opposite direction.”

Aldric’s expression hardens. “I know the grounds.”

“Then this is worse than I thought.” She goes out, papers tucked against her silver hair.

Seraphel’s smile turns briefly private before she follows Aldric into the common room.

Thessaly watches the doorway close behind them. “He has decided walking elsewhere is studying.”

“It may be a religious exercise,” says one of the servers, collecting a wineglass.

Thessaly considers that. “Then I hope it works.”

Beyond the garden doors, Ashara and Rashid cross the pale path toward the octagon. Their voices carry only in fragments before the wind takes them: Rashid objecting to something; Ashara’s shorter reply; then the wooden practice blades knocking together in a quick, hard rhythm.

Thessaly sets down the spoon she has been turning.

“Dena is coming here with Oren and Mara,” she says. “Cards, apparently. Rashid is meant to join them after drills.” Her gaze passes over the cleared table, not quite settling anywhere. “I may play if there is a fourth seat. I don’t like watching games whose rules I don’t know.”

A little later, the common room’s fire brightens as a servant adds wood. The house divides itself into its evening: song at the chapel, studying in the library, blades at the octagon, cards soon enough by the hearth.
If Ashara is still nearby, I ask whether an untrained partner would be any use for practice. If she has already left, I let the opportunity pass.

Ashara is already beyond the garden doors, her dark figure moving beside Rashid along the pale path. A practice blade knocks sharply against another, then again. You let the thought go unsaid.

Thessaly rises from the table and smooths her sleeve.

“They’ll be here shortly,” she says, meaning Dena and the card players. “I’m going to learn the rules before anyone claims I cheated.”

She heads for the common room, where the fire throws a broad amber glow over the chairs. Outside, Ashara and Rashid’s drills continue: quick footfalls, wood striking wood, Rashid’s brief laugh carried in through the partly open garden door.
I accept whatever answer she has given and leave her plans alone. I finish my meal rather than following anyone to practice.

You remain at the table while the servers clear around you. The last bite of tart is sharp with berries and less sweet than it looks.

Outside, the practice blades keep their quick, regular rhythm for several minutes, then stop. You hear no argument afterward—only the garden door opening and closing somewhere beyond the hall.

From the common room comes a new cluster of voices. A young woman says, “If anyone mentions my wrist before I’ve had a card in my hand, I’m leaving,” followed by a man’s immediate, “Noted,” and a woman’s laugh.

Thessaly answers, “What are the rules?”

“Bad luck and worse judgment,” Dena says. “You’ll learn.”

The fire pops. Cards begin to shuffle.

At the dining-hall doorway, a server pauses with the coffee tray. “Would you like some, Mr. Garvey?”
I go to the house library and look on the open shelves for an introductory book about the Council. If I need help finding one, I ask whoever is working there.

The common room has settled into its second life by the time you pass through it. Cards snap against the low table by the fire. Dena, her splinted wrist resting carefully on a cushion, studies her hand with theatrical suspicion while Thessaly holds her own cards too upright to conceal anything.

“I understand the rules,” Thessaly says. “I dislike them.”

“You’ve played three hands,” Dena replies.

“That was enough.”

No one looks up for more than a moment as you continue to the library.

Its air smells of lamp oil, old bindings, and the faint mineral damp that clings to the Academy in storm weather. An iron spiral stair winds up through the center of the room. Open shelves rise on both levels, their sections marked in seven scripts; the nearby volumes concern treaty law, arbitration, Council proceedings, and commentaries dense enough to make the shelf sag.

Caelindra occupies one end of a long reading table beneath a green-shaded lamp. A stack of notes sits precisely squared at her elbow. She does not look up when you enter.

At the reference desk, an older human man in a dark, ink-marked coat is making notes in a ledger. He notices you studying the shelves and then the signet at your hand.

“You’re Rowan Garvey,” he says. “Gareth Stone. I teach human Covenant history.”

The organization turns out to be less helpful than it first appears: the Academy considers “introductory” material a subset of constitutional theory, while the most accessible-looking books are actually arguments about centuries-old tariff disputes. After a few minutes, you ask Stone for help.

He gets up without ceremony and leads you to a lower shelf near the desk. “Start here.”

He draws out a slim green volume with a worn gilt title: *The Council at Work: A Conclave Primer.*

“It covers the seven seats, committees, votes, arbitration, and the ways a treaty becomes binding. It will tell you what people mean when they use the phrases as if everyone was born knowing them.”

From the reading table, Caelindra turns a page.

“It calls the voting arrangement equitable,” she says. “Then puts the exceptions in a footnote forty pages later.”

Stone glances toward her. “Forty-one.”

“An improvement, then.”

He hands you the book. Its first page bears a neat Academy stamp and a list of former Conclave readers, none of the names familiar.

“Read the first three chapters,” Stone says. “After that, you’ll know enough to recognize when someone is explaining the Council to you selectively.”
Once I have a book, I settle down and read quietly for half an hour.

The primer is dry, but useful. Over the next half-hour, its diagrams make the Council’s machinery clearer: seven seats, committees that handle disputes before they reach a full vote, arbitration panels, and the treaties that bind each territory to the others. The human seat has remained formally vacant for sixty years, its duties distributed by provisional arrangements that now have to be reconsidered.

The book gives Article Nineteen a short, bloodless paragraph among the Covenant’s founding restrictions. Enforcement belongs to the Council and local courts; no exception is described.

At the next table, Caelindra turns pages with swift, impatient precision. Stone works through his ledger until the library clock marks the half hour.

From the common room comes the sound of the garden door opening, then Rashid’s voice: “I know I’m late. Deal me in before Thessaly rewrites the rules.”

“I have improved them,” Thessaly replies.

Dena laughs. “That’s exactly what I was afraid of.”

Stone closes his ledger and looks toward the shelves of Council records. “The primer’s honest enough for a beginning,” he says. “The arguments start after chapter three.”
As I read, I silently wonder whether my aunt once kept a blue glass bird on her desk. I do not say this aloud; it is only a private guess. I return my attention to the page.

No one reacts to the thought you keep to yourself.

You turn back to the primer. Its next section explains the Council’s committees: trade, borders, education, reparations, and the smaller arbitration panels where most disputes are meant to end before they become speeches in the full chamber. The language is calm enough to make every old compromise sound inevitable.

Across the table, Caelindra closes one book and draws another from her stack.

“The primer is least misleading on procedure,” she says without looking at you. “Do not mistake that for neutrality.”

Professor Stone reshelves a returned volume near the desk. Beyond the library doors, the card game breaks into a burst of laughter, then a groan from Rashid.

The green-shaded lamp pools steadily over the page as you continue reading.
I take a short break in the common room. If Seraphel is there and not occupied in a conversation, I ask, "What do you like reading for pleasure?" Otherwise I sit with my book.

Seraphel has not returned from the chapel. You take a leather chair near the fire and open the primer across your knee.

At the low table, Dena plays one-handed with practiced irritation, her splinted wrist supported on a cushion. Rashid has been dealt into the game at last; he studies his cards while Thessaly watches Mara’s turn with grave concentration.

“You can’t change the value of a card halfway through,” Dena says.

“I haven’t,” Thessaly replies. “I have clarified its potential.”

“That is changing it.”

Rashid’s mouth twitches. “I’m beginning to understand why no one invites fae to tax negotiations.”

The fire settles with a soft collapse of coals. You read while the game continues around you, occasionally punctuated by Dena’s dry complaints and the shuffle of cards.
If we are talking, I ask Seraphel what she likes about her choice. If she has chosen not to talk, I let her be and read.

Seraphel is still at the chapel, so the question waits.

You read by the fire while the card game turns increasingly argumentative. Thessaly has not improved the rules, whatever she claims; Dena wins another hand one-handed and accepts the victory with a satisfied, “There. Civilization endures.”

Rashid groans and gathers the cards for the next deal. The primer stays open across your knees, its account of committees and provisional human duties steady in the firelight.
I let the conversation end naturally and return to my book. I stay with it until I finish the chapter.

The chapter ends with the provisional arrangements made after the human seat fell vacant: other delegates may administer certain duties, but none may vote or speak as the human representative. Your arrival has made several “temporary” practices suddenly subject to review.

At the card table, Dena wins once more, then gathers her cards with a pleased little exhale.

“That’s enough charity for one evening.”

“It wasn’t charity,” Rashid says.

“It never is when you lose.”

Mara and Oren help her to her feet without fuss. Rashid walks them as far as the front hall, promising Dena he will look over the revised practice schedule tomorrow. She gives him a look that suggests she will hold him to it.

Thessaly remains by the fire, sorting the cards into unnervingly exact piles. The library waits quietly beyond the open doors, and somewhere upstairs the house settles around its new human heir.
I go to bed when I am done reading. The next morning I wash, dress, and get breakfast in time for the scheduled orientation.

Morning brings the low blue light of storm clouds and the scent of fresh bread downstairs.

You wash, dress in the charcoal coat, and make it to breakfast with time to spare. Ashara and Rashid are already at the table, arguing quietly over a point from last night’s drills.

“Your guard opened on the third exchange,” Ashara says.

“It adjusted.”

“It opened.”

Rashid looks across the table at you. “Morning, Rowan. The eggs are safe. Avoid the pale sauce unless you enjoy regretting things before noon.”

Thessaly has a small stack of cards beside her plate, arranged in rigid suits and ranks. “Dena explained the rules again. They remain inefficient.”

“They’re cards,” Caelindra says from behind a book.

“Then they could be better cards.”

At the ninth bell, the residents make their way across the quadrangle to the Conclave seminar room. Lightning moves slowly beneath the far bridges, far enough below that the storm seems almost decorative.

Inside, fifteen chairs surround the oval table, though only seven are occupied. The framed Accords on the walls carry the Covenant in scripts you cannot read. Aldric chooses a place facing the door; Ysolde takes a seat near an open window where the cold air reaches her. Ashara and Rashid sit apart, still conducting their argument in occasional glances.

Professor Elara Windwhisper enters precisely on the bell. Her silver hair is braided close to her head, and she carries no notes.

“Welcome to the Conclave,” she says. “For four years, you will study the structure you may someday be asked to preserve, amend, or survive.”

She looks around the table, including you without lingering on the Garvey signet.

“Today is orientation. We will cover Academy procedure, residence expectations, access privileges, and the first term’s work. Tomorrow, you begin Covenant Law.”

She takes the remaining chair at the head of the oval table and opens a thin folder.

Outside, another branch of lightning blooms beneath the Nexus.
At orientation, I ask how a student in the human seat is supposed to learn the practical duties of the role.

Professor Windwhisper looks up from her folder.

“How is a student in the human seat meant to learn its practical duties?” you ask.

“A necessary question, Mr. Garvey.” Her voice is quiet enough that the room stills to hear it. “In an ordinary year, a Conclave heir arrives with tutors, family records, and a predecessor whose work can be observed. You have none of those advantages.”

Rashid shifts slightly in his chair.

Windwhisper continues. “You are a Conclave student, not yet a sitting Council delegate. This term will give you Council procedure, treaty interpretation, negotiation exercises, committee memoranda, and supervised study of prior proceedings. Professor Stone will oversee the surviving human historical material available to students.”

Caelindra taps one finger against her notes. “Available is doing a great deal of work there.”

“It usually does,” Windwhisper says. “Restricted histories require the Chancellor’s signature, regardless of the student requesting them.”

She turns a page.

“The human seat’s former functions have been divided provisionally among existing offices and committees. You will receive a current list of those functions, their holders, and the legal basis for each arrangement by noon. You should learn not only what the seat once did, but what others have done in its absence.”

“Will he receive the reports sent to it?” Rashid asks. “Or only the account prepared after someone decides what he needs to know?”

“Procedural reports relevant to his course work, yes,” says Windwhisper. “Private Council correspondence, no. The same boundary applies to every student here.”

“That seems reasonable,” Ashara says. “He needs to know where authority is actually being exercised, not be handed a ceremonial history and told he is prepared.”

Ysolde looks toward the framed Accords. “Some duties can be returned. Others will need to be negotiated again.”

Thessaly rests her hands on the table. “And whoever has held them may believe they have terms.”

Aldric’s posture grows a little straighter. “The Council has procedures for resolving that.”

Rashid glances at him. “Procedures are not the same as willingness.”

Before the exchange can sharpen, Seraphel speaks softly.

“An office absent still shapes each choice and voice;  
Learn where its silence borrows someone’s voice.”

Windwhisper inclines her head, accepting the point without comment.

“Precisely. Mr. Garvey, your practical education will include learning where the human seat’s absence has become convenient, necessary, or contested. The Academy can teach you the structure. Judgment will require more than a primer.”

She closes the folder.

“Now: residence expectations. Garvey House is shared Conclave housing. Its history does not grant any resident authority over another resident’s room, correspondence, or private affairs.”

The orientation moves on, but the promised list now has a place in the morning ahead of you.
I listen to the answer and then let the next person speak.

Rashid speaks next.

“Will the list distinguish treaty obligations from habits that became convenient while the seat was empty?”

Professor Windwhisper regards him for a moment. “Yes. Each arrangement will include its stated authority, term, and review process. Where an office has exceeded its temporary mandate, the record should make that visible.”

“Should,” Caelindra says.

“It will,” Windwhisper replies.

Rashid nods once, satisfied enough to let the matter rest.

The orientation continues through practical matters: seminar attendance, formal notices, access to the quadrangle after curfew, and the need to register any travel beyond the Nexus bridges. Windwhisper mentions the dueling grounds only to clarify that rankings carry no automatic authority in Conclave proceedings.

Ashara leans back slightly at that. “A tragic administrative error.”

“It may be corrected by demonstrating better judgment in committee,” Windwhisper says.

A few seats away, Ysolde studies the printed term schedule. “The border arbitration exercise lasts six weeks.”

“It does.”

“That is short.”

“For an exercise.”

Ysolde accepts this with a quiet nod, though not approval.

By the time the bell marks the end of orientation, a packet awaits at each place: course schedules, Academy maps, residence rules, and—set apart in a sealed grey envelope—a memorandum addressed to Rowan Garvey concerning the current administration of the human seat’s duties.
After orientation I check the public dueling schedule. If I can watch Ashara's ranked bout, I take a place as a spectator; if it has already finished, I look at the posted result.

The dueling schedule is posted on a slate board beside the octagon, its white lettering refreshed by a hovering lamp-globe.

**Eleventh bell — Ranked bout, first tier:** Ashara vel Kothren vs. Tovan Rimeclaw.

You have time.

By the eleventh bell, a loose crowd has gathered along the low rail around the packed-earth octagon. The storm lies far below the terrace, turning the sky beneath the plateau a bruised silver. Ashara waits inside the ring in padded black practice armor, her tied hair damp at the temples and a blunted sword balanced loosely in one hand.

Her opponent is broad-shouldered and furred along the jaw and forearms, wearing blue wraps over one elbow. He gives Ashara a polite nod before taking his guard.

Rashid stands near the rail, arms folded. He notices you arrive but keeps his attention on the ring.

The signal sounds.

Tovan opens hard, trying to drive her backward with his size. Ashara gives him ground for three steps, then changes the angle so abruptly that his next strike meets empty space. Her practice blade raps his ribs. Once. Twice.

The crowd makes the small approving noise of people who recognize clean work.

Tovan adjusts, more cautious now. He catches her next attack, forces her blade low, and nearly lands a touch at her shoulder. Ashara twists away; her tail lashes for balance, and she comes back inside his reach before he can reset. The flat of her blade strikes his wrist. His weapon falls into the dirt.

The second signal ends it.

Tovan retrieves his sword and bows with visible annoyance, though he says something that makes Ashara’s mouth briefly curve. The ranking clerk marks the result beside the slate: **Kothren retains first tier.**

Rashid exhales through his nose. “Her third exchange was better than yesterday.”

Ashara steps out of the octagon, accepts a towel from an attendant, and catches sight of you among the spectators. Her gaze rests there for a moment before she turns back to the clerk to sign the result.
Afterward I spend an hour walking in the gardens on my own. I do not seek anyone out.

The gardens keep their own weather. Pale paths curve between flowering hedges and low stone walls that blunt the wind from the plateau’s edge; beyond them, lightning turns silently beneath the Nexus.

You walk without choosing a destination. White blossoms close their cups against the cool air, while red climbing flowers have found the warmth of a sun-facing wall. A pair of older students pass at the far end of a path, deep in an argument about trade tariffs, and disappear toward the quadrangle without noticing you.

Near the library wall, an unmarked door sits recessed behind a veil of ivy. It is plainly old, its metal handle dull with neglect. Nothing about it invites interruption, and you continue on.

By the time a distant bell marks the hour, you have looped back toward Garvey House. The garden doors stand ahead, reflecting the pale afternoon light.
I return to the common room. If Rashid is there and not busy, I ask how his evening went. Otherwise I leave him to it.

Rashid is alone near the common-room fire, his practice jacket folded over one arm of the chair and a cup of tea cooling on the table beside him. He looks up when you enter.

You ask how his evening went.

He smiles, showing a hint of canine. “Dena won three hands one-handed and acted surprised every time. Thessaly tried to amend the scoring halfway through a deal. Mara threatened to make her play face-up.”

He takes a sip of tea. “I arrived late, lost what little dignity I had left after drills, and was told it was a lesson in priorities. Dena was in excellent spirits, so I suppose it went well.”

The fire clicks softly between you.
I settle down with my book again. I do not volunteer to sort out anyone else's arrangements.

You settle into a leather chair by the fire and reopen *The Council at Work*.

The next chapter concerns arbitration: who may request it, who appoints its panels, and how a dispute can spend years being called temporary while everyone involved learns to live around it. The prose is not elegant, but it is clear enough.

Rashid lets the silence stand. After finishing his tea, he gathers a small stack of papers from the side table—practice schedules, by the look of them—and checks several names against a notebook before folding the pages together.

“I’ve got correspondence to answer,” he says. “Enjoy the thrilling machinery of civilization.”

He leaves through the hall with the papers under his arm.

The fire burns low and steady. Beyond the common room, Garvey House carries on around you: a door shuts upstairs, someone crosses the dining hall, and the stormlight below the windows shifts from white to a muted violet as you read.
At the next communal meal I take an available seat. If Seraphel is there, I ask whether she knows a song worth learning; otherwise I listen to the table.
